title: SpeakOut Student Wellbeing Guide
subtitle: A practical guide to mental health, confidence, resilience, relationships, and personal growth
author: SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach
description: A flagship SpeakOut handbook designed to help students understand wellbeing, manage stress, build confidence, develop healthy relationships, and create a personal wellbeing plan.
content:
Chapter 1: Welcome to SpeakOut

Your Wellbeing Journey Begins

Wellbeing is the overall state of your emotional, mental, social and physical health while you live, learn and grow. It is not a fixed trait you either have or lack — it moves throughout the week depending on sleep, stress, relationships and what is happening in your life. Everyone's wellbeing needs attention sometimes, not just people going through an obvious crisis.

This course introduces the ideas, language and practical skills covered in the SpeakOut Student Wellbeing Handbook. Each module pairs a short lesson with a reflection activity and a short knowledge check, so you can build understanding gradually rather than all at once.

There is no requirement to share anything personal with anyone else to complete this course. The reflection questions are for your own thinking; what matters for completion is that you engage honestly with the material and pass each knowledge check.

If anything in this course brings up something you are struggling with, that is a normal and valid response — not a sign you are doing the course wrong. Module 15 covers how and when to ask for support, and you do not have to wait until then to reach out to a trusted adult, school counsellor or local mental health service if you need to.

Take a few quiet minutes with these questions. There are no right answers — they are here to help you notice where you already are before the course begins.

  1. What does wellbeing mean to you?
  2. Which area of your wellbeing needs the most attention right now?
  3. Who are three trusted people you can talk to?

Reflection

  1. What does wellbeing mean to you?
  2. Which area of your wellbeing needs the most attention right now?
  3. Who are three trusted people you can talk to?

Chapter 2: What Is Mental Health?

Understanding the foundation

Mental health refers to your emotional, psychological and social wellbeing — it shapes how you think, feel, handle stress, relate to others and make decisions. Like physical health, everyone has mental health, and it exists on a spectrum rather than as a simple “healthy” or “unhealthy” label. It can be strong in some seasons of life and more fragile in others.

A common myth is that mental health struggles mean something is “wrong” with a person, or that only certain people experience them. In reality, mental health difficulties are common and can affect anyone, regardless of age, background or how someone appears on the outside. Struggling does not mean weakness, and it is not something a person chooses.

Another myth is that mental health only matters once things become severe. In practice, small, regular habits — sleep, movement, connection with others, and having language to describe how you feel — support mental health long before a crisis point, in the same way brushing your teeth prevents problems rather than only treating them.

This course does not diagnose or treat any condition. It offers general education, language and coping skills. If you are ever concerned about your own mental health or someone else's, speak with a trusted adult, school counsellor or qualified professional.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What mental health myths have you heard?
  2. How can schools make it safer for students to speak up?
  3. What is one fact about mental health you want others to know?

Reflection

  1. What mental health myths have you heard?
  2. How can schools make it safer for students to speak up?
  3. What is one fact about mental health you want others to know?

Chapter 3: Knowing Yourself

Self-awareness and growth

Self-awareness is the ability to notice your own thoughts, feelings, values and patterns of behaviour — and to understand how they affect your choices. It is a skill, not a fixed personality trait, which means it can be practised and strengthened over time.

One useful starting point is identifying your strengths: the things you are naturally good at or that come easily to you. Strengths are not only academic or athletic — they include things like listening well, staying calm under pressure, being organised, or making others feel included.

Values are what matters most to you — honesty, fairness, family, creativity, achievement, and so on. When your daily choices line up with your values, you tend to feel more grounded; when there is a gap between what you value and how you are actually spending your time, that gap is often a source of stress worth noticing.

Self-awareness also includes recognising habits you would like to change. Growth does not require becoming a different person — it means noticing a pattern, understanding what triggers it, and choosing one small, realistic adjustment at a time.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What are three strengths you have?
  2. What value matters most to you?
  3. What is one habit you want to improve?

Reflection

  1. What are three strengths you have?
  2. What value matters most to you?
  3. What is one habit you want to improve?

Chapter 4: Understanding Emotions

Naming, accepting, and managing feelings

Emotions are signals — they give you information about what is happening in your life and what you might need. All emotions, including uncomfortable ones like anger, sadness, jealousy or fear, are normal and serve a purpose. The goal is not to eliminate difficult emotions but to recognise, name and respond to them in healthy ways.

Naming an emotion accurately — for example, noticing that what feels like anger is actually hurt, or that anxiety is layered under excitement — tends to make it easier to manage. This is sometimes called “emotional vocabulary,” and it grows with practice, the same way any vocabulary does.

Accepting an emotion means acknowledging it is present without judging yourself for feeling it. This is different from acting on every emotional impulse. You can feel intense anger and still choose how you respond — the feeling and the action are two separate steps.

Healthy ways to manage strong emotions include pausing before reacting, physical movement, talking to someone you trust, writing your thoughts down, and slow breathing. What works varies from person to person, so it is worth trying a few approaches to find what genuinely helps you.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. Which emotion do you find hardest to express?
  2. What helps you calm down safely?
  3. How can you express anger without hurting yourself or others?

Reflection

  1. Which emotion do you find hardest to express?
  2. What helps you calm down safely?
  3. How can you express anger without hurting yourself or others?

Chapter 5: Managing Stress

Pressure, coping, and balance

Stress is your body and mind's response to pressure or demand — exams, deadlines, family responsibilities, or social situations. In small amounts, stress can be motivating and help you focus. Problems tend to arise when stress is constant, feels unmanageable, or has no outlet.

A useful first step in managing stress is identifying your specific triggers. Stress is easier to respond to once you can name what is actually causing it, rather than experiencing it as one large, vague weight.

Healthy coping strategies include breaking large tasks into smaller steps, planning your time realistically, physical activity, sufficient sleep, and talking to someone about what is on your mind. Coping strategies that provide short-term relief but add long-term harm — such as avoiding responsibilities entirely, or using substances to numb stress — tend to make the underlying pressure worse over time.

It is also worth noticing when a responsibility feels too big to face. Breaking it into smaller, concrete steps — the next single action rather than the whole task — usually makes it feel more manageable and reduces the urge to avoid it altogether.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What are your top three stress triggers?
  2. What is one healthy coping skill you can practice this week?
  3. What responsibility can you break into smaller steps?

Reflection

  1. What are your top three stress triggers?
  2. What is one healthy coping skill you can practice this week?
  3. What responsibility can you break into smaller steps?

Chapter 6: Anxiety and Worry

Calming the mind

Anxiety is your body's alarm system — it prepares you to respond to a perceived threat, even when the “threat” is a test, a social situation, or an uncertain future rather than immediate physical danger. Occasional worry is a normal part of life. It becomes more difficult to manage when it is frequent, intense, or interferes with daily activities like sleeping, eating or attending school.

Anxiety often shows up physically — a racing heart, tight chest, upset stomach, or restlessness — before it is fully recognised as a thought. Learning to notice these body signals early can help you respond before worry escalates.

Grounding techniques help bring attention back to the present moment when worry feels overwhelming. Common examples include slow, deliberate breathing; naming five things you can see, four you can hear and three you can touch; or focusing on a single physical sensation, like your feet on the floor.

Occasional worry is manageable with these everyday tools. If anxiety is frequent, intense, or is stopping you from doing things you need or want to do, that is a signal worth taking seriously — it is appropriate and encouraged to speak with a trusted adult, school counsellor or qualified mental health professional.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What does worry feel like in your body?
  2. Which grounding technique can you try?
  3. When should someone seek extra support for anxiety?

Reflection

  1. What does worry feel like in your body?
  2. Which grounding technique can you try?
  3. When should someone seek extra support for anxiety?

Chapter 7: Building Resilience

Recovering from setbacks

Resilience is the ability to recover, adapt and keep functioning after a setback, disappointment or difficult experience. It is often misunderstood as never struggling — in reality, resilience is about how you respond and recover after struggle, not about avoiding hardship altogether.

Resilience is built, not simply inherited. Factors that strengthen it include having supportive relationships, developing problem-solving skills, practising self-compassion instead of harsh self-criticism, and maintaining a sense that your actions can make a difference in your own life.

Reframing a setback — asking “what can I learn from this?” instead of only “why did this happen to me?” — does not erase the disappointment, but it can shift a setback from feeling purely like failure to feeling like useful information for next time.

Recovering from a setback also does not mean pretending it did not hurt. Acknowledging the disappointment honestly, giving yourself time, and then identifying one next step is usually more sustainable than forcing immediate positivity.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. Describe a setback you survived.
  2. What helped you recover?
  3. What lesson did you learn from that experience?

Reflection

  1. Describe a setback you survived.
  2. What helped you recover?
  3. What lesson did you learn from that experience?

Chapter 8: Healthy Relationships

Respect, boundaries, and communication

Healthy relationships — friendships, family relationships, and romantic relationships — share common features: mutual respect, honesty, trust, and the ability to disagree without the relationship being threatened. No relationship is conflict-free; what distinguishes a healthy one is how conflict is handled.

A boundary is a limit you set about what you are and are not comfortable with — how you want to be spoken to, how much time you can give, or what topics you are willing to discuss. Setting a boundary is not the same as rejecting a person; it is a normal, healthy part of any relationship, and people who respect you will generally respect your boundaries too.

Respectful communication includes listening without interrupting, using “I feel” statements instead of blame, and checking that you have understood the other person before responding. These skills reduce the chance that a disagreement escalates unnecessarily.

Warning signs of an unhealthy relationship include consistent disrespect, control over who you see or what you do, pressure to do things you are uncomfortable with, and refusal to accept a boundary once it has been clearly stated. If you notice these patterns in your own relationships, it is worth talking to a trusted adult.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What does respect look like in friendship?
  2. What boundary do you need to set?
  3. How can you handle conflict more calmly?

Reflection

  1. What does respect look like in friendship?
  2. What boundary do you need to set?
  3. How can you handle conflict more calmly?

Chapter 9: Self-Esteem and Confidence

Seeing yourself with value

Self-esteem is the overall sense of your own worth, while confidence often refers more specifically to belief in your ability to handle a particular task or situation. Both can fluctuate — it is normal to feel confident in one area of life and unsure in another.

A common obstacle to healthy self-esteem is the “inner critic” — an automatic negative thought pattern that exaggerates flaws or mistakes. Learning to notice these thoughts and question whether they are actually accurate, rather than accepting them automatically, is a core self-esteem skill.

Confidence tends to build through action rather than waiting to feel ready first. Small, achievable steps — trying something new, speaking up once, completing a task you were avoiding — create real evidence of capability that gradually builds belief in yourself.

Comparing yourself to others, especially on social media where people typically only share their highlights, tends to distort self-esteem. It is more useful to compare your progress to your own past, rather than to someone else's curated presentation of their life.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What negative thought do you need to challenge?
  2. What is one thing you are proud of?
  3. What action can build your confidence this week?

Reflection

  1. What negative thought do you need to challenge?
  2. What is one thing you are proud of?
  3. What action can build your confidence this week?

Chapter 10: Digital Wellbeing

Social media, safety, and balance

Digital wellbeing is about how technology and social media affect your mood, sleep, relationships and sense of self — and making intentional choices about your use, rather than using devices purely on autopilot.

Social media often shows a curated highlight reel rather than everyday reality. Comparing your ordinary day to someone else's best moments is an unfair comparison that can quietly affect mood and self-esteem over time, even when you know intellectually that it is not a complete picture.

Practical digital wellbeing habits include noticing how you feel during and after scrolling, setting boundaries around screen use before bed (screen light and stimulating content can interfere with sleep), being selective about who and what you follow, and taking deliberate breaks from platforms that consistently leave you feeling worse.

Online safety also matters: protecting personal information, being cautious about who you share images or details with, and recognising and reporting cyberbullying — whether it happens to you or someone you know — rather than assuming it must be dealt with alone.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. How does social media affect your mood?
  2. What digital habit do you want to change?
  3. How can you protect yourself online?

Reflection

  1. How does social media affect your mood?
  2. What digital habit do you want to change?
  3. How can you protect yourself online?

Chapter 11: Study Skills and Balance

Learning without burnout

Effective studying is less about the number of hours spent and more about how that time is used. Techniques like spacing study sessions out over several days (rather than cramming), testing yourself on material instead of just re-reading it, and studying in short focused blocks with real breaks tend to produce better results with less exhaustion.

Burnout is a state of physical and mental exhaustion caused by prolonged pressure without adequate recovery. Early signs include persistent tiredness even after resting, declining motivation, irritability, and finding it harder to concentrate than usual. Recognising these signs early makes them easier to address before they become severe.

Balance does not mean never working hard — it means making sure rest, sleep, movement and connection with others have a genuine place alongside your responsibilities, rather than being treated as optional extras only allowed once everything else is finished.

Realistic weekly planning — writing down what actually needs to happen and roughly when, rather than keeping it all in your head — tends to reduce the background anxiety of feeling like you might be forgetting something important.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What study habit works best for you?
  2. What is one sign you may need rest?
  3. How can you plan your week better?

Reflection

  1. What study habit works best for you?
  2. What is one sign you may need rest?
  3. How can you plan your week better?

Chapter 12: Physical Health and Mental Health

The body-mind connection

Physical health and mental health are closely connected — what affects the body tends to affect mood, concentration and emotional regulation, and vice versa. This is sometimes called the body-mind connection, and it is one of the most well-established general ideas in wellbeing education.

Sleep is one of the most influential factors. Insufficient or irregular sleep is linked to lower mood, reduced concentration and greater difficulty managing stress. A consistent sleep routine — similar bedtime and wake time most days — tends to support both physical and mental wellbeing more than occasional long “catch-up” sleep.

Regular movement, even in modest amounts like walking, tends to support mood and stress management, partly through its physical effects and partly by providing a break from other pressures. It does not need to mean intense exercise to be beneficial.

Nutrition and hydration also play a role — skipping meals or being significantly dehydrated can affect concentration, energy and irritability. None of these habits are a cure for a mental health condition on their own, but they are a meaningful, practical foundation that supports overall wellbeing.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. How many hours do you sleep on most nights?
  2. What physical habit affects your mood?
  3. What small health habit can you improve?

Reflection

  1. How many hours do you sleep on most nights?
  2. What physical habit affects your mood?
  3. What small health habit can you improve?

Chapter 13: Purpose and Goals

Direction, motivation, and meaning

A sense of purpose — having something that feels meaningful to work toward — is associated with greater motivation and resilience during difficult periods. Purpose does not need to be a single grand life mission; it can be as immediate as a value you want to live by this year, or a skill you want to develop.

Goals turn a general sense of direction into something actionable. Clear goals tend to specify what exactly you are working toward, and over what timeframe, rather than staying vague (“I want to do better” versus “I want to improve my grade in this subject by the end of term”).

Large goals can feel overwhelming or distant, which is why breaking them into smaller milestones — and identifying the very next concrete step — makes consistent progress far more achievable than waiting for motivation to arrive fully formed.

It is also normal for goals and sense of purpose to shift over time as you learn more about yourself. Revisiting and adjusting your goals periodically is a sign of healthy self-awareness, not a sign of failure or inconsistency.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What kind of person do you want to become?
  2. What goal matters to you this term?
  3. What is the first small step?

Reflection

  1. What kind of person do you want to become?
  2. What goal matters to you this term?
  3. What is the first small step?

Chapter 14: Helping a Friend

Support without carrying everything alone

Being a supportive friend does not require having all the answers. Often, the most valuable thing you can offer is genuine listening — giving someone your full attention, not interrupting to fix or minimise what they are sharing, and letting them know you believe them and are glad they told you.

Supporting a friend is different from carrying their problem for them. You can care deeply about someone without taking full responsibility for solving what they are going through — especially situations that need adult or professional support, such as abuse, self-harm, or thoughts of suicide.

Some problems should never be kept secret, even if a friend asks you to promise not to tell anyone. If a friend's safety is at risk — for example, they mention self-harm, suicide, abuse, or another situation where someone could be seriously hurt — the caring and responsible response is to tell a trusted adult, even though it may feel like breaking their trust in the moment. A safe friend is not always a silent one.

If you are supporting a friend through something difficult, it is also important to look after your own wellbeing and talk to a trusted adult yourself — you do not have to carry it entirely alone either.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. How can you listen better?
  2. What problem should never be kept secret?
  3. Who can help if a friend is unsafe?

Reflection

  1. How can you listen better?
  2. What problem should never be kept secret?
  3. Who can help if a friend is unsafe?

Chapter 15: Asking for Help

Strength, safety, and support

Asking for help is a sign of self-awareness and strength, not weakness — it means recognising a limit and taking a responsible step to address it, which is exactly what people with strong problem-solving skills do. The idea that people should always manage alone is a myth that stops many people from getting support earlier, when it is often easier to help.

Signs that someone may need extra support include noticeable changes in mood, sleep, appetite, or behaviour that last more than a couple of weeks; withdrawing from friends and activities they used to enjoy; a persistent sense of hopelessness; or, seriously, talking about wanting to harm themselves or not wanting to be here anymore. These signs apply both to noticing them in yourself and in others.

Common reasons students hesitate to ask for help include fear of being judged, not wanting to be a burden, not knowing who to ask, or believing the problem is not “serious enough.” None of these are good reasons to stay silent — support is available for a wide range of concerns, not only severe ones.

Trusted people to reach out to include a parent or guardian, a teacher or school counsellor, another trusted adult in your life, or a qualified mental health professional. If you or someone you know is in immediate danger, contact local emergency services right away.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What signs show someone may need help?
  2. Who are your trusted support people?
  3. What stops students from asking for help?

Reflection

  1. What signs show someone may need help?
  2. Who are your trusted support people?
  3. What stops students from asking for help?

Chapter 16: Your Personal Wellbeing Plan

Turning learning into action

A personal wellbeing plan turns everything covered in this course into something practical you can actually use — rather than information you read once and forget. It does not need to be complicated; a short, honest plan you will actually follow is more useful than an elaborate one you abandon after a week.

A useful wellbeing plan usually includes: your early warning signs (the first signals that your stress or mood is slipping, from earlier modules), a short list of coping tools that genuinely work for you, the names of two or three trusted people you can reach out to, and one or two small daily or weekly habits you want to keep consistent — such as sleep routine, movement, or check-ins with a friend.

Reviewing your plan occasionally — monthly, or after a stressful period — and adjusting it as you learn more about what works for you keeps it useful rather than letting it become outdated.

Completing this course is a starting point, not a finish line. Wellbeing is an ongoing practice, and it is normal to keep learning, adjusting, and reaching out for support as your circumstances change.

Reflect honestly on these questions, and consider writing your answers down somewhere you can return to.

  1. What are your early warning signs?
  2. What coping tools work for you?
  3. What commitments will you make for the next 30 days?

Reflection

  1. What are your early warning signs?
  2. What coping tools work for you?
  3. What commitments will you make for the next 30 days?

title: Teacher Wellbeing and Safeguarding Guide
subtitle: A practical classroom guide to prevention, early support, safe conversations and referral
author: SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach
description: An in-depth field guide for educators who want to build psychologically safer classrooms, notice changes early, respond without diagnosing, follow safeguarding duties and protect their own wellbeing.

chapters.title: Mental health belongs in everyday teaching
chapters.content:
Teachers influence the climate in which young people learn and seek help. This chapter establishes a practical, non-clinical understanding of mental health so educators can promote wellbeing without stepping outside their role.

Mental health is the ongoing state of your emotional, psychological, and social wellbeing — it shapes how you think, feel, cope with pressure, relate to the people around you, and make decisions large and small. Just as everyone has physical health, whether they are currently sick or well, everyone has mental health, whether they currently feel steady or shaky. It is not a category reserved for people with a diagnosed condition, and it does not divide neatly into "healthy" and "unhealthy." Instead, picture it as a wide spectrum you move along over time, influenced by what is happening in your life and how well-supported you feel while it happens.

One of the most important things to understand is that mental health is not fixed. It can shift meaningfully from one week to the next depending on how much sleep you are getting, how heavy your workload feels, the state of your relationships, financial pressure, physical illness, or a single major life event like a loss or a big transition. It is entirely possible to be functioning well in most areas of your life — doing fine at school or work, keeping up with friends — while genuinely struggling in one specific area, like sleep or motivation. That is not a contradiction or a sign that you are faking one side of it. It is simply how mental health actually works for most people, most of the time.

It also helps to separate ordinary distress from a diagnosable condition. Not every hard week, disappointing month, or emotionally heavy season reflects a mental health disorder. At the same time, someone who does live with a diagnosed condition can still have long stretches where they function well, feel like themselves, and enjoy their life. Diagnosis itself is a clinical judgment that takes training, time, and context a single conversation cannot provide — it is not something you should attempt on yourself, a friend, or a family member, no matter how many symptoms seem to match something you read online.

Why does this distinction matter so much in practice? Because treating every low mood as an emergency, and dismissing every real struggle as "not serious enough to matter," both cause harm in different directions. The first can make you or people around you feel alarmed or over-managed for normal human ups and downs. The second can leave a genuine, worsening problem unspoken and unsupported until it becomes much harder to address. A more useful habit is learning to notice patterns rather than reaching for a label: how long has this lasted, how intense does it feel, and how much is it actually interfering with sleep, relationships, schoolwork, or daily functioning.

If you are ever unsure whether what you or someone else is experiencing is "serious enough" to bring up, treat that uncertainty itself as a reason to talk to someone rather than a reason to wait. A trusted adult, a school counselor, or a mental health professional can help sort out what is happening far better than guesswork, and reaching out early is never the wrong call. The goal of this course is not to turn you into a diagnostician for yourself or anyone else — it is to help you notice honestly, respond calmly, and know when and how to bring in real support.

Put it into practice

Write two or three sentences describing your own definition of mental health, then note whether it has changed after this lesson.

chapters.title: Emotions, behaviour and the learning environment
chapters.content:
Behaviour communicates needs, but it never tells the whole story. Use this chapter to distinguish observation from assumption and to respond with curiosity, predictable boundaries and dignity.

Self-awareness is the ability to notice your own thoughts, feelings, and behavior patterns as they are happening, rather than only recognizing them afterward, once a reaction has already played out. It is worth stating clearly: this is a skill that improves with deliberate practice, not a fixed trait that some people are simply born with and others are permanently without. Anyone can build it, though it takes consistent attention over time rather than a single insight.

A useful place to start is noticing physical signals. Emotions frequently register in the body before they are consciously recognized as thoughts — a tightening chest, a clenched jaw, restless legs, a racing heart, shallow breathing. These physical cues often arrive earlier than the thought "I am anxious" or "I am angry" does. Learning to notice them as they build, rather than only once a full emotional reaction is underway, gives you meaningfully more choice in how you respond, because you are catching the signal closer to its source.

Building a short pause between noticing a strong feeling and reacting to it is one of the most practical tools available here. Even a few seconds — taking one slow breath, silently naming what you are feeling, stepping back half a step in a tense conversation — interrupts the automatic reaction that would otherwise take over. This pause does not eliminate the feeling or make it disappear. It creates a small window in which a more deliberate, considered response becomes possible instead of the first impulsive one.

Journaling and regular reflection build this skill over a longer timeframe. Writing down, even briefly, what you felt in a given moment and what seemed to trigger it creates a record you can look back on — something memory alone tends to distort or forget. Over weeks, patterns start to emerge: certain situations, people, or times of day that reliably produce certain reactions in you. Recognizing these patterns in writing is far easier than trying to recall them from memory under pressure, and it turns self-awareness from a vague aspiration into something you can actually track.

Self-awareness is not about constant self-monitoring or judging yourself harshly for every reaction. It is about building enough distance from your own immediate experience to notice it clearly, which in turn makes it easier to respond thoughtfully rather than automatically. If you notice a pattern that concerns you — a reaction that feels disproportionate, or a physical signal that shows up constantly and will not settle — that is worth bringing to a trusted adult or professional rather than working through entirely on your own. Self-awareness is meant to help you understand yourself better, not to replace real support when you need it.

Put it into practice

For the next two situations that trigger a strong emotional reaction, practice pausing for five seconds before responding, and note what changed about your reaction.

chapters.title: Recognising stress before it becomes a crisis
chapters.content:
Stress can affect attendance, concentration, memory, relationships and conduct. The teacher's task is to notice meaningful change, document facts and open a safe route to support—not to diagnose.

Stress is the body and mind's response to demands that feel like they require more than you currently have readily available. It is not a character flaw or a sign of weakness — it is a built-in alarm system that evolved to help you respond quickly to threats and challenges. When something demanding shows up, whether it is a real danger or just a looming deadline, your nervous system reacts in largely the same way, because it was not designed to tell the difference between a physical threat and a stressful email.

In the short term, this response can actually work in your favor. Your heart rate rises, muscles tense, breathing quickens, and your attention narrows and sharpens. Blood flow shifts toward the muscles and away from processes like digestion that are not urgent in the moment. Before a presentation, a game, or a deadline sprint, this surge of activation can help you move faster, think quickly, and perform under pressure. This is why a small amount of stress often feels energizing rather than purely unpleasant — your body is doing exactly what it is supposed to do.

The trouble starts when this high-alert state does not get a chance to switch off. The body is built for stress to arrive in waves, with recovery in between, not for the alarm to stay on for days, weeks, or months at a stretch. When stress runs too long without enough recovery, people commonly notice fatigue that sleep does not fully fix, irritability that seems to arrive faster than usual, trouble falling or staying asleep, tension headaches, a tight jaw or shoulders, and difficulty concentrating on things that used to feel simple. None of these are signs that something is broken in you — they are signs that your system has been running in overdrive without enough time to reset.

It also helps to remember that stress is not a fixed, universal quantity. The exact same demand — a pop quiz, a conflict with a friend, a busy week at work — can affect two people quite differently, depending on how much else is already on their plate, what coping resources and support they have access to, how much sleep and stability they are working with, and how they interpret the situation itself. Someone who has a lot of unresolved stress already stacked up will often feel a new demand hit much harder than someone who is otherwise well-rested and supported. This is worth remembering both about yourself and about other people — you rarely know the full stack someone else is carrying.

Learning to notice your own stress response as it is happening, rather than only recognizing it in hindsight, is one of the most useful skills this course will build toward. If stress ever feels like it has become constant, overwhelming, or connected to thoughts of hopelessness or not wanting to go on, that is a sign to reach out to a trusted adult, a school counselor, or a mental health professional right away rather than trying to manage it alone.

Put it into practice

Keep a one-day log of physical sensations (tense shoulders, racing thoughts, tiredness) whenever you notice stress rising, and note what triggered each one.

chapters.title: Teaching practical regulation skills
chapters.content:
Short grounding and breathing practices can help a class settle and can give an overwhelmed learner enough space to make a safer next choice. They should be offered, not forced, and never used as punishment.

Regulation skills exist to help reduce the intensity of an anxious spiral so that you can think and act more deliberately, rather than being swept along by the reaction. Slow breathing, sensory grounding, and deliberate attention-shifting are practical, learnable tools, but like most skills, they work best when you have practiced them regularly ahead of time, not only when you reach for them for the first time in a moment of maximum distress.

When multiple demands pile up at once, it can feel like everything needs to happen immediately — the assignment, the chore, the message you have not replied to, the commitment you agreed to weeks ago that is now due tomorrow. But even though everything can feel equally pressing in the moment, not everything is actually equally urgent or equally important, and treating every task the same way is one of the fastest routes to feeling overwhelmed.

It helps to draw a real distinction between urgent and important, because the two get blurred together constantly. Urgent tasks demand immediate attention — a deadline today, a time-sensitive request. Important tasks matter for your longer-term goals and wellbeing, whether or not they come with a ticking clock — things like maintaining relationships, taking care of your health, or working steadily toward a bigger goal. A simple sorting method can cut through the noise quickly. List out everything currently on your plate, then sort each item into one of four categories: urgent and important, important but not urgent, urgent but not important, and neither urgent nor important. chapters.title: Digital wellbeing, privacy and trust
chapters.content:

Every time an app asks for access to your location, contacts, camera, or microphone, that request is a real decision worth pausing on, not a formality to tap through as quickly as possible to get to what you actually wanted to do. Permissions determine what an app can see and collect about you long after the initial installation, often continuing quietly in the background well beyond the moment you granted access.

A useful habit is asking whether a given permission request actually makes sense for what the app claims to do. A flashlight app requesting access to your contacts and precise location has no functional reason to need either one to turn your camera's light on, which should raise an immediate question about why it's asking. When a permission request doesn't clearly match the app's actual purpose, that mismatch is worth taking seriously rather than dismissing as normal, even if the app seems otherwise legitimate and widely used.

It also helps to know that permissions aren't usually a one-time, irreversible decision made at installation. Most phones let you review and individually turn off permissions for any app well after you've already installed and started using it, typically through a privacy or permissions section in your device settings. Periodically going through this list and checking which apps currently have access to your camera, microphone, contacts, or location is a healthy, ongoing habit rather than an excessive or paranoid one — it's the digital equivalent of occasionally checking which spare keys to your home are still floating around.

Default settings tend to favor broader data collection rather than your privacy, and it's worth understanding why. Many apps are built around business models where more access to your data, activity, or location translates directly into value for the company behind the app, whether through advertising, analytics, or other data-driven purposes. That means the most permissive default settings usually benefit the app more than they benefit you, and there's often little incentive built into the app's design to nudge you toward more restrictive, privacy-protective options on your own.

Grant only the permissions an app genuinely needs to function, decline or revoke the rest, and revisit the full list every so often as apps update and your own usage changes over time. Review the permissions on three apps on your phone. Revoke at least one permission that doesn't match what the app actually needs to function.

chapters.title: Responding to persistent low mood
chapters.content:
A parent should take sustained changes seriously without rushing to label them. Focus on observable changes, listen, reduce shame and seek qualified support when symptoms persist or daily functioning declines.

Everyone experiences sadness at various points — it is a normal, expected emotion, not something to be avoided or treated as a problem. Clinical depression is different, and the difference lies mainly in duration, intensity, and impact rather than simply in how "sad" someone feels. Understanding this distinction helps you respond appropriately, both to yourself and to people around you, instead of either dismissing something serious or treating every low mood as an emergency.

Ordinary sadness typically has an identifiable cause — a disappointment, an argument, a loss — and it tends to ease as circumstances change or as time passes. Depression behaves differently. It tends to persist for weeks or longer, often without a single clear trigger you can point to, and it usually affects more than mood alone: motivation, sleep, appetite, energy, and concentration are frequently affected alongside how someone feels emotionally. This broader, more persistent pattern is what separates depression from a difficult week or a bad month.

It is also important to know that depression does not always look like visible sadness. It can present as irritability or a short temper, emotional numbness or flatness, persistent exhaustion that does not improve with rest, a noticeable loss of interest in activities that used to be enjoyable, or difficulty concentrating on things that used to feel easy. Because it can look so different from person to person — and does not always match the crying, withdrawn stereotype many people expect — it is often missed, both by the person experiencing it and by people around them.

Dismissing genuine depression as someone simply "being sad" or needing to "snap out of it" can leave a real, worsening problem unaddressed for far too long. On the other hand, treating every ordinary low mood as a medical emergency can create unnecessary alarm and, over time, make it harder to take real warning signs seriously when they do appear. Neither extreme is helpful.

What actually helps is paying attention to duration and impact rather than reaching for a label. Ask honestly: how long has this lasted, and how much is it affecting daily functioning — sleep, relationships, schoolwork, basic motivation? If the answer suggests this has gone on for weeks rather than days, and is meaningfully interfering with everyday life, that is worth raising with a trusted adult, school counselor, or mental health professional, since diagnosing depression is a clinical judgment that requires proper training, not something to determine from a checklist alone.

Write down two or three signs that would distinguish ordinary sadness from something that might need more attention.

chapters.title: Building a family support and referral plan
chapters.content:
Support is easier to access when families identify trusted adults, school contacts, health professionals and emergency routes before a crisis. Make the plan visible, specific and appropriate to your location.

After you've looked out for safety and listened without pressure, the Link step often starts somewhere surprisingly unglamorous: practical help. It's tempting to think that the most meaningful part of PFA is the emotional conversation, but in the actual moment, a glass of water, a place to sit down, or help making a phone call can matter more to someone than any amount of talking about feelings. Practical needs and emotional needs aren't competing with each other — meeting the practical ones often makes space for the emotional ones to settle.

Practical help can mean a lot of different things depending on the situation: accurate, simple information about what's happening or what happens next, a quiet place to sit, help contacting a family member, or arranging transport somewhere safe. None of these require special training to provide, but they require you to notice that they're needed, which is easy to miss if you're focused entirely on saying the right comforting words.

Rather than guessing at what someone needs, it's almost always more effective to ask directly: "what would be most helpful right now?" This does two things at once — it gets you accurate information instead of a guess, and it hands a small piece of control back to someone whose sense of control may have just been badly shaken. Being asked what they need, rather than having help decided for them, can itself be part of what helps someone feel steadier.

You don't need to solve every problem the person is facing, and trying to would set an unrealistic and exhausting standard for yourself. Helping with one concrete task — finding a charger, locating a restroom, tracking down a phone number — can meaningfully reduce someone's distress even though it looks small from the outside. Small, completed help is often more valuable than an ambitious offer that never quite comes together, so don't underestimate the modest, doable thing you can actually follow through on.

List five types of practical help a PFA helper might offer someone right after a distressing event.

A simple sorting method can cut through the noise quickly. List out everything currently on your plate, then sort each item into one of four categories: urgent and important, important but not urgent, urgent but not important, and neither urgent nor important. This exercise usually takes only a few minutes, but it tends to reveal something useful almost immediately — often that the thing generating the most anxiety is not actually the most important item on the list, and that something genuinely important has been quietly pushed aside because it never felt urgent enough to demand attention.

Once things are sorted, the plan often becomes obvious: handle what is urgent and important first, schedule specific time for what is important but not urgent so it does not get permanently deprioritized, and look for ways to delegate, shorten, or simply let go of what falls into the urgent-but-not-important and neither categories.

It is worth remembering, especially under real pressure, that a reasonable plan acted on beats a perfect plan that takes too long to create. You do not need to sort every task with total precision or build an elaborate system. The goal is simply to get enough clarity to start moving on the right things first, rather than freezing or bouncing between tasks based on whichever one feels loudest in the moment.

Digital wellbeing, privacy and trust

Online life is part of adolescent life. Effective family safety combines practical privacy habits with ongoing conversation, so a young person can ask for help after a mistake without fearing an explosive response.

Every time an app asks for access to your location, contacts, camera, or microphone, that request is a real decision worth pausing on, not a formality to tap through as quickly as possible to get to what you actually wanted to do. Permissions determine what an app can see and collect about you long after the initial installation, often continuing quietly in the background well beyond the moment you granted access.

A useful habit is asking whether a given permission request actually makes sense for what the app claims to do. A flashlight app requesting access to your contacts and precise location has no functional reason to need either one to turn your camera's light on, which should raise an immediate question about why it's asking. When a permission request doesn't clearly match the app's actual purpose, that mismatch is worth taking seriously rather than dismissing as normal, even if the app seems otherwise legitimate and widely used.

It also helps to know that permissions aren't usually a one-time, irreversible decision made at installation. Most phones let you review and individually turn off permissions for any app well after you've already installed and started using it, typically through a privacy or permissions section in your device settings. Periodically going through this list and checking which apps currently have access to your camera, microphone, contacts, or location is a healthy, ongoing habit rather than an excessive or paranoid one — it's the digital equivalent of occasionally checking which spare keys to your home are still floating around.

Default settings tend to favor broader data collection rather than your privacy, and it's worth understanding why. Many apps are built around business models where more access to your data, activity, or location translates directly into value for the company behind the app, whether through advertising, analytics, or other data-driven purposes. That means the most permissive default settings usually benefit the app more than they benefit you, and there's often little incentive built into the app's design to nudge you toward more restrictive, privacy-protective options on your own.

Adjusting these settings after installing something new typically takes only a few minutes, and it's a habit worth building into how you set up any new app rather than treating as a one-time project. Grant only the permissions an app genuinely needs to function, decline or revoke the rest, and revisit the full list every so often as apps update and your own usage changes over time. Many phones also let you grant location or microphone access only while an app is actively in use, rather than all the time, which is a good middle ground for apps that have a legitimate but occasional need for that data.

Responding to persistent low mood

A parent should take sustained changes seriously without rushing to label them. Focus on observable changes, listen, reduce shame and seek qualified support when symptoms persist or daily functioning declines.

Everyone experiences sadness at various points — it is a normal, expected emotion, not something to be avoided or treated as a problem. Clinical depression is different, and the difference lies mainly in duration, intensity, and impact rather than simply in how "sad" someone feels. Understanding this distinction helps you respond appropriately, both to yourself and to people around you, instead of either dismissing something serious or treating every low mood as an emergency.

Ordinary sadness typically has an identifiable cause — a disappointment, an argument, a loss — and it tends to ease as circumstances change or as time passes. Depression behaves differently. It tends to persist for weeks or longer, often without a single clear trigger you can point to, and it usually affects more than mood alone: motivation, sleep, appetite, energy, and concentration are frequently affected alongside how someone feels emotionally. This broader, more persistent pattern is what separates depression from a difficult week or a bad month.

It is also important to know that depression does not always look like visible sadness. It can present as irritability or a short temper, emotional numbness or flatness, persistent exhaustion that does not improve with rest, a noticeable loss of interest in activities that used to be enjoyable, or difficulty concentrating on things that used to feel easy. Because it can look so different from person to person — and does not always match the crying, withdrawn stereotype many people expect — it is often missed, both by the person experiencing it and by people around them.

This distinction matters in practice because getting it wrong causes harm in two different directions. Dismissing genuine depression as someone simply "being sad" or needing to "snap out of it" can leave a real, worsening problem unaddressed for far too long. On the other hand, treating every ordinary low mood as a medical emergency can create unnecessary alarm and, over time, make it harder to take real warning signs seriously when they do appear. Neither extreme is helpful.

What actually helps is paying attention to duration and impact rather than reaching for a label. Ask honestly: how long has this lasted, and how much is it affecting daily functioning — sleep, relationships, schoolwork, basic motivation? If the answer suggests this has gone on for weeks rather than days, and is meaningfully interfering with everyday life, that is worth raising with a trusted adult, school counselor, or mental health professional, since diagnosing depression is a clinical judgment that requires proper training, not something to determine from a checklist alone.

Building a family support and referral plan

Support is easier to access when families identify trusted adults, school contacts, health professionals and emergency routes before a crisis. Make the plan visible, specific and appropriate to your location.

After you've looked out for safety and listened without pressure, the Link step often starts somewhere surprisingly unglamorous: practical help. It's tempting to think that the most meaningful part of PFA is the emotional conversation, but in the actual moment, a glass of water, a place to sit down, or help making a phone call can matter more to someone than any amount of talking about feelings. Practical needs and emotional needs aren't competing with each other — meeting the practical ones often makes space for the emotional ones to settle.

Practical help can mean a lot of different things depending on the situation: accurate, simple information about what's happening or what happens next, a quiet place to sit, help contacting a family member, or arranging transport somewhere safe. None of these require special training to provide, but they require you to notice that they're needed, which is easy to miss if you're focused entirely on saying the right comforting words.

Rather than guessing at what someone needs, it's almost always more effective to ask directly: "what would be most helpful right now?" This does two things at once — it gets you accurate information instead of a guess, and it hands a small piece of control back to someone whose sense of control may have just been badly shaken. Being asked what they need, rather than having help decided for them, can itself be part of what helps someone feel steadier.

You don't need to solve every problem the person is facing, and trying to would set an unrealistic and exhausting standard for yourself. Helping with one concrete task — finding a charger, locating a restroom, tracking down a phone number — can meaningfully reduce someone's distress even though it looks small from the outside. Small, completed help is often more valuable than an ambitious offer that never quite comes together, so don't underestimate the modest, doable thing you can actually follow through on.
